title: Sensor Dictionary Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: The robot dictionary from Chapter 5 drawn as a cabinet of labeled drawers. Students read, update, and add entries by key, see each action as a line of MicroPython with its printed output, and trigger a KeyError for a missing key.

educational.topic: Dictionaries: reading, updating, and adding key-value pairs
learningObjectives: Read a dictionary value with its key, such as robot["speed"].
Update an existing value and add a new key with the same assignment syntax.
Predict a KeyError when code reads a key that is not in the dictionary.
Explain why named keys can be easier to read than list indexes.
standards: CSTA 2-AP-11: Create clearly named variables that represent different data types and perform operations on their values

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Guided practice with immediate feedback and an error-first challenge
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Students choose a key and a value, then press Read, Update value, or Add new key; the matching MicroPython line, printed output, and a plain-language explanation appear.
keyQuestions: How do you read the robot's speed from the dictionary?
What happens when you read a key that does not exist?
Why does robot["battery_pct"] = 85 add a key instead of causing an error?
Which is easier to understand: robot_list[1] or robot["speed"]?
commonMisconceptions: Reading a missing key returns None or 0 instead of raising a KeyError.
Dictionaries are read by position, like robot[1].
Adding a new key needs a special method instead of a normal assignment.
Updating a value changes the key's name.
assessmentOpportunities: Record the value and data type for each starting key.
Challenge: fix a KeyError without changing the read line.
Exit ticket: write one update line and one add line for the robot dictionary.
